slots.practicalActivity: In the Azure Portal, create a real Storage account (Standard performance, LRS redundancy, StorageV2 kind) and enable the hierarchical namespace setting during creation so it becomes an ADLS Gen2 account instead of plain Blob storage, then download one month of real NYC Taxi trip CSV data from the TLC's public site to use for the rest of this course.
slots.deliverable: A live Azure ADLS Gen2 storage account (StorageV2, hierarchical namespace enabled) visible in the portal, plus one downloaded real NYC Taxi trip CSV file on your machine.

slots.practicalActivity: In your storage account, create one container named taxi-data, then build a nested folder path inside it (e.g. raw/yellow-taxi/year=2024/month=01/) using Storage Explorer or the portal's file browser, and rename one folder to confirm the hierarchical namespace makes that an atomic operation instead of a blob-prefix simulation.
slots.deliverable: One real container (taxi-data) containing a nested, Hive-style folder path, with a note confirming a folder rename completed as a single atomic operation.

slots.practicalActivity: Assign yourself the Storage Blob Data Contributor RBAC role at the storage-account level, then set a directory-level ACL on just one folder inside taxi-data, confirming the difference in scope between account-wide RBAC and one-directory ACLs; separately, create an Azure Managed Identity and note which future resource would use it to reach this account without a stored secret.
slots.deliverable: A real RBAC role assignment on the storage account, one directory-scoped ACL entry on a single folder, and a created Managed Identity, with a written note on when each access method applies.

lessons.title: CSV vs. JSON vs. Parquet vs. Delta

slots.practicalActivity: Generate a real, time-limited, read-only SAS token scoped to the taxi-data container and test it by opening the generated URL, then convert your downloaded taxi CSV to Parquet with a quick pandas df.to_parquet(...) call and compare the two files' sizes on disk.
slots.deliverable: A tested, read-only SAS URL that successfully retrieves a blob, plus a Parquet version of the taxi CSV with a written file-size comparison against the original CSV.

slots.practicalActivity: Upload your taxi data into the raw/yellow-taxi/year=2024/month=01/ Hive-style partition path you built earlier, then sketch your own full container-to-partition path for a second, different dataset applying all five lake-design decisions, and create processed/ and curated/ sibling folders next to raw/ for it.
slots.deliverable: Real taxi data correctly Hive-partitioned under raw/, a written full-path sketch for a second dataset covering all five design decisions, and a created three-zone (raw/processed/curated) folder skeleton.

slots.practicalActivity: Manually copy your Parquet file from the previous slot into the processed/cleansed zone you created, then write a one-paragraph note mapping your raw/processed/curated folders onto the Bronze/Silver/Gold naming and describing what would still need to happen to that file before it reaches curated/Gold.
slots.deliverable: The Parquet file placed in the correct middle zone of your data lake, plus a written Bronze/Silver/Gold mapping and a note on what's needed before the final zone.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter lab: without new instruction, build one complete real data lake for a second month of NYC Taxi data from scratch — container, Hive-style partitioned raw zone, an RBAC or ACL assignment, and a converted Parquet file sitting in a processed zone — reusing every decision from this chapter end to end.
slots.deliverable: A second month of real NYC Taxi data correctly organized through a full raw-to-processed data lake structure in your Azure storage account, with access control applied, closing out Chapter 1.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Python 3.10+ and VS Code if you haven't already, open a new folder for this course's exercises, create first_script.py, and run the lesson's two-line script printing a fare amount and passenger count, confirming output appears in VS Code's integrated Terminal panel.
slots.deliverable: A working first_script.py run successfully from inside VS Code, with its printed output visible in the Terminal panel.

slots.practicalActivity: In a new variables.py file, declare variables for one real taxi trip's fare_amount (float), passenger_count (int), vendor_id (string), and a boolean for whether it was a credit-card payment, then print each value and its type() to confirm Python's type inference.
slots.deliverable: A variables.py script printing four correctly typed variables modeling one real taxi trip field each, with type() output confirmed in the Terminal.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a Python list of 5 dictionaries, each representing one taxi trip with keys for fare_amount, trip_distance, and passenger_count using believable values, then write a list comprehension that extracts just the fare_amount values into a new list.
slots.deliverable: A script holding a list of 5 trip dictionaries and a separately extracted list of their fare amounts, both printed to the Terminal.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the 5-trip list of dictionaries, write a for loop that prints only trips where fare_amount is greater than $10 and passenger_count is at least 2, with an if/elif/else inside the loop labeling each trip 'short', 'medium', or 'long' by trip_distance.
slots.deliverable: A script that loops over the 5 trips, prints only those matching the fare/passenger filter, and labels each short/medium/long by distance.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: extend the 5-trip list to 10 trips by hand, then write a loop that computes and prints the total fare, the average fare, and the count of trips longer than 3 miles, using only the conditions, loops, lists, and variables covered so far.
slots.deliverable: A script printing the total fare, average fare, and long-trip count across 10 hand-built trip records.

slots.practicalActivity: Refactor the fare-total/average/long-trip logic from the previous slot into three functions (total_fare(trips), average_fare(trips), count_long_trips(trips, threshold)), each taking the trips list as a parameter and returning a value, then call all three on the same 10-trip list.
slots.deliverable: A refactored script with three working functions replacing the previous slot's inline loop logic, producing identical results when called.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a deliberately bad trip record to your list (fare_amount as the string 'N/A') and wrap your total_fare() function's math in a try/except block that catches the resulting TypeError, printing a clear warning and skipping that record instead of crashing.
slots.deliverable: A script that runs to completion on a list containing one deliberately invalid record, printing a caught-exception warning for it instead of crashing.

slots.practicalActivity: Write your 10-trip list of dictionaries out to a real local CSV file by hand using the open()/write() pattern (or Python's csv module), then open and read that same file back line by line, printing each row.
slots.deliverable: A real local CSV file written by your script, plus confirmation it was read back and each row printed correctly.

slots.practicalActivity: Install pandas (pip install pandas), load the CSV file from the previous slot into a DataFrame with pd.read_csv(), and run .head(), .describe(), and .info() on it to compare pandas's view of your data against the raw dictionaries you built by hand.
slots.deliverable: A script that loads your hand-built CSV into a pandas DataFrame and prints the output of .head(), .describe(), and .info().

slots.practicalActivity: Load the real NYC Taxi CSV from Chapter 1 using pd.read_csv() with parse_dates for the pickup/dropoff timestamp columns and an explicit dtype for VendorID, then export the DataFrame to a JSON file and read that JSON back into a second DataFrame, confirming both match.
slots.deliverable: The real taxi CSV correctly loaded with parsed dates and explicit dtypes, exported to JSON, and re-read into a second DataFrame matching the first.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: using the real taxi DataFrame from the previous slot, filter it down to trips with fare_amount > 0 and passenger_count > 0, drop duplicate rows, and print the row count before and after — a small-scale rehearsal of this chapter's upcoming full ETL script.
slots.deliverable: A written before/after row count showing the real taxi DataFrame successfully filtered and deduplicated.

slots.practicalActivity: Install the requests library and write a script that calls a free public REST API (e.g. a weather or exchange-rate API) with requests.get(), checks response.status_code, and parses the JSON response with .json(), printing two or three fields from the result.
slots.deliverable: A working script that successfully calls a real public REST API and prints parsed fields from its JSON response.

slots.practicalActivity: Take the nested JSON response captured from the previous slot's API call, write it to a local .json file, then load it back with Python's json module and write code that navigates at least two levels of nesting to pull out one specific value.
slots.deliverable: A local JSON file and a script that successfully extracts one value from at least two levels of nesting inside it.

slots.practicalActivity: Connect to a real local database (sqlite3, built into Python, is fine), create a small taxi_trips table, and insert 3-5 rows from your pandas DataFrame using a parameterized INSERT statement rather than string concatenation.
slots.deliverable: A real local SQL database containing a taxi_trips table populated with rows inserted from Python using parameterized queries.

slots.practicalActivity: On the full real taxi DataFrame, chain cleaning operations end to end: .dropna(subset=[...]) on required columns, boolean filters removing non-positive fares/distances, .drop_duplicates(), and a new fare_per_mile column, printing the row count after each step.
slots.deliverable: A cleaning script on the real taxi data printing the row count after each of the four cleaning steps, with a final fare_per_mile column confirmed present.

lessons.title: Building a Simple Python ETL Process

slots.practicalActivity: Build the chapter finale's exact three-function ETL script (extract/transform/load) against your own real taxi CSV, writing the cleansed result to a Parquet file in your Chapter 1 data lake's processed zone, and confirm the printed row count in the load() function's output.
slots.deliverable: A working extract/transform/load Python script run end to end against real taxi data, producing a Parquet file in a processed zone with a printed final row count.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter capstone lab: extend the ETL script to accept a list of multiple source CSV paths (e.g. two different months of taxi data) and loop over them, writing one output Parquet file per month, plus add one new validation rule of your own, such as rejecting trips over 100 miles as likely data errors.
slots.deliverable: An extended ETL script that processes two real source CSV files into two separate cleansed Parquet outputs, including one self-authored validation rule beyond the original four, closing out Chapter 2.

slots.practicalActivity: Try loading an unrealistically large stand-in for the full historical NYC Taxi dataset (concatenate many copies of your CSV, or reason through the real multi-year file count and row totals) into a single pandas DataFrame, and observe or calculate where memory or time would actually give out, confirming exactly where Chapter 2's Pandas approach stops working.
slots.deliverable: A written note on what happened (or would happen) when attempting to load an unrealistically large taxi dataset with pandas, tying it directly to why Spark exists.

slots.practicalActivity: Install PySpark locally (pip install pyspark, requires a JDK), start a SparkSession, and open the Spark UI (usually localhost:4040 while a job runs) to find your own driver and executor listed under the Executors tab, even running in local mode.
slots.deliverable: A locally running Spark session with the Spark UI's Executors tab open, showing at least a driver and one executor for your own installation.

slots.practicalActivity: Load the real taxi Parquet file from Chapter 2 into a Spark DataFrame, call .rdd.getNumPartitions() to see its current partition count, then explicitly .repartition(4) it and re-check the count, confirming Spark's own partitioning is a separate concept from Chapter 1's storage-level Hive partitioning.
slots.deliverable: A script showing the real taxi data's Spark partition count before and after an explicit repartition call.

slots.practicalActivity: Chain three transformations (.filter(), .select(), .withColumn()) onto the taxi Spark DataFrame without calling any action, and confirm in the Spark UI that no job has actually run yet; then call .count() as an action and watch a real job appear and complete in the UI.
slots.deliverable: A before/after note from the Spark UI showing zero completed jobs after chaining transformations, then one completed job immediately after calling an action.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a clean, minimal script that explicitly creates a SparkSession with SparkSession.builder.appName(...).getOrCreate(), uses it to read the real taxi Parquet file, and calls .printSchema() and .show(5) to confirm the session is correctly wired to real data.
slots.deliverable: A minimal script with an explicit SparkSession successfully reading real taxi data, with its schema and first 5 rows printed.

slots.practicalActivity: Register your real taxi Spark DataFrame as a temp view with .createOrReplaceTempView('trips'), then run one aggregation using DataFrame method chaining (e.g. .groupBy('VendorID').avg('fare_amount')) and the same aggregation written as a Spark SQL string, confirming both produce identical results.
slots.deliverable: Two equivalent query results (DataFrame API and Spark SQL) against the same real taxi data, confirmed to match.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter lab: load a full month of real taxi data into Spark, register it as a temp view, and write three original Spark SQL queries of your own (e.g. busiest pickup hour, highest-earning vendor, average trip distance by passenger count), checking at least one result against the equivalent pandas calculation from Chapter 2.
slots.deliverable: Three original Spark SQL queries run successfully against a full month of real taxi data, with one result cross-checked against Chapter 2's pandas output, closing out Chapter 3.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a small Spark DataFrame manually from a Python list of hand-built taxi trips using spark.createDataFrame(), then separately read the real taxi CSV with spark.read.csv(..., header=True, inferSchema=True), comparing the manual DataFrame's schema against the inferred one from the real file.
slots.deliverable: A manually created small Spark DataFrame and a separately loaded real taxi CSV DataFrame, with a written note comparing their schemas.

slots.practicalActivity: Export a small sample of your taxi data to JSON from pandas and read it into Spark with spark.read.json(), then read the Parquet file you produced in Chapter 2's ETL lab with spark.read.parquet(), comparing inferred schema correctness across the three formats (CSV, JSON, Parquet) you've now read into Spark.
slots.deliverable: The same taxi data successfully read into Spark from JSON and Parquet, with a written comparison against the earlier CSV read.

slots.practicalActivity: Define an explicit PySpark StructType schema naming every taxi column and its correct type (timestamps, doubles for fares, integers for passenger_count), then re-read the real taxi CSV passing schema=your_schema instead of inferSchema=True, confirming .printSchema() now shows your exact types.
slots.deliverable: An explicit StructType schema and a CSV read using it, with .printSchema() output confirming the exact types you defined.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: using wildcard path syntax (e.g. spark.read.csv('taxi-data/raw/yellow-taxi/*/*/*.csv')), read every partitioned CSV file from your Chapter 1 data lake's raw zone directly into one Spark DataFrame in a single call, confirming the row count matches the sum of each individual month's file.
slots.deliverable: One Spark DataFrame loaded via a wildcard path from multiple real partitioned files, with its total row count confirmed against the sum of the individual files.

slots.practicalActivity: On the real taxi DataFrame, use .select() to keep only pickup/dropoff timestamps, fare_amount, and trip_distance, then chain .filter() to keep only rows with fare_amount > 2.50 and trip_distance > 0, printing the row count before and after filtering.
slots.deliverable: A narrowed, filtered real taxi DataFrame with a printed before/after row count from the filter step.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a computed fare_per_mile column with .withColumn() (fare_amount divided by trip_distance), then add a trip_tier column using when()/otherwise() labeling each row 'short' (<2 mi), 'medium' (2-10 mi), or 'long' (>10 mi), and run .groupBy('trip_tier').count().
slots.deliverable: The real taxi DataFrame with two new columns (fare_per_mile and trip_tier) and a printed count of trips in each tier.

slots.practicalActivity: Cast the VendorID column from string to integer with .cast(), and on a text column (or a small added sample column of vendor names with inconsistent casing/whitespace), apply .trim(), .upper() or .lower(), and one more string function to produce a cleaned version.
slots.deliverable: The real taxi DataFrame with VendorID cast to integer and one text column cleaned via chained string functions, confirmed with .printSchema() and .show().

slots.practicalActivity: Extract pickup_hour and pickup_dayofweek columns from the pickup timestamp using Spark's hour() and dayofweek() functions, then find and handle any null passenger_count values with .na.fill() or .na.drop(), reporting how many rows were affected.
slots.deliverable: The real taxi DataFrame with two new date-derived columns and a written count of how many rows had null passenger_count values, now handled.

slots.practicalActivity: Deliberately union the real taxi DataFrame with itself to create exact duplicate rows, confirm the inflated row count, then call .dropDuplicates() and confirm the row count returns exactly to the original pre-union number.
slots.deliverable: A before/after row count showing duplicates correctly introduced and then fully removed with .dropDuplicates().

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter practice: combine this chapter's techniques so far into one cleaning pipeline — select the relevant columns, filter out bad fares/distances, cast VendorID, add fare_per_mile and trip_tier, extract pickup_hour, handle nulls, and drop duplicates — all chained in one script against a full month of real taxi data.
slots.deliverable: One chained cleaning pipeline script combining at least six Chapter 4 techniques, run successfully end to end against a full month of real taxi data.

slots.practicalActivity: Group the cleaned taxi DataFrame by VendorID and pickup_hour, and compute avg(fare_amount), sum(trip_distance), and count(*) for each group using .agg(), printing the results sorted by hour.
slots.deliverable: A grouped, multi-metric aggregation result (average fare, total distance, trip count by vendor and hour) printed in sorted order.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a small zones lookup DataFrame (a handful of pickup location IDs mapped to borough names, hand-typed), left-join it to the taxi DataFrame on PULocationID, then load a second month of real taxi data and .union() it onto the first month's cleaned DataFrame, confirming the combined row count.
slots.deliverable: The taxi DataFrame successfully left-joined to a zones lookup table, plus two months of real taxi data combined via .union() with a confirmed combined row count.

slots.practicalActivity: Using pyspark.sql.window.Window partitioned by pickup date and ordered by fare_amount descending, apply rank() or row_number() to find the single highest-fare trip on each day across your two-month combined dataset.
slots.deliverable: A window-function query result showing the top-fare trip for each distinct pickup date in your dataset.

slots.practicalActivity: Register the two-month combined DataFrame as a temp view, then rewrite the earlier groupBy aggregation (vendor/hour averages) as a Spark SQL query string instead of DataFrame methods, confirming both approaches return the same numbers.
slots.deliverable: A Spark SQL rewrite of an earlier DataFrame aggregation, confirmed to match the original DataFrame-method result.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the final cleaned, joined dataset to Parquet with .write.mode('overwrite').partitionBy('pickup_year','pickup_month').parquet(...), then inspect the output folder structure to confirm Spark created separate partition subfolders matching the partitionBy columns, just as Chapter 1 designed by hand.
slots.deliverable: A real Parquet output on disk, partitioned by pickup_year and pickup_month, with the folder structure confirmed to match the partition columns.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the course finale's performance lab for real: .cache() the cleaned DataFrame and confirm a second action reuses it (check the Spark UI's Storage tab), then join it against the small zones lookup table wrapped in broadcast(), and write the final result partitioned by pickup_year/pickup_month, comparing the join's .explain() plan with and without broadcast().
slots.deliverable: A cached DataFrame visible in the Spark UI's Storage tab, plus a broadcast join whose .explain() plan is confirmed to differ from a non-broadcast version of the same join.

slots.practicalActivity: Course capstone: build one original, complete pipeline from scratch — read raw NYC Taxi CSV files from your Chapter 1 data lake's raw zone with an explicit schema, clean and enrich them with at least five Chapter 4 transformations, join in the zones lookup with a broadcast join, cache the intermediate result, and write the final output as partitioned Parquet into the curated zone — tying together all four chapters of this course into one end-to-end pipeline.
slots.deliverable: One original, end-to-end PySpark pipeline script, run successfully against real NYC Taxi data from raw read through to a cached, broadcast-joined, partitioned Parquet write in the curated zone, closing out Data Engineering Foundations.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can design a zoned Azure data lake, write real Python ETL scripts, and build a complete hands-on PySpark pipeline — reading, cleaning, joining, and writing partitioned data — against real NYC Taxi data, the foundation every later course in the Data Engineering track builds directly on.
